Project Charter · Brady Household · August 15, 2026

who’s making dinner?

A household decision system for the one question that gets asked every single night — named for the fictional 1970s sitcom in HBO’s Hacks, built for the real family that argues about it at 5 PM.

Sponsor & operator Kyle Early user Marissa Panel Hudson · Rowan · Dylan Agent Stitch (phase 3)
1

The Charter

problem → hypothesis → experiment
1.1

Problem statement

Every evening between 4:30 and 6:00 PM, a five-person household faces the same unresolved question. The central problem is not lack of effort — it is misalignment between what the household buys, what it cooks, and what it ultimately orders or improvises. Groceries are purchased without a meal attached to them; meals are chosen at the lowest-energy moment of the day with no prepared options; the outcome is decided by whoever caves first.

That misalignment shows up daily as avoidable uncertainty, and the fallback — delivery takeout — resolves the evening while quietly failing the week.

1.2

Impact profile

Dinner decisions quietly consume four household resources. None of them appears on a receipt, which is why the problem persists.

ResourceHow it drainsVisible symptom
TimeThe same deliberation re-run nightly from scratchDecision stretches across the whole 5 PM hour
MoneyUnplanned takeout; groceries bought without intent that expire unusedTakeout spend; food waste
EnergyDecision arrives exactly when the deciders are most depleted“I don’t care, you pick” loops
GoodwillConflicting preferences with no shared memory of what workedThe nightly negotiation; split-outcome nights

A fifth resource — health — degrades as a consequence: fallback meals are systematically less balanced than intended meals. The household's standing "Meal Planning Automation" scope (the family Holy Grail project, Feb 2026) set the ambition this charter operationalizes: less waste, less takeout, and “what’s for dinner” answered in under a minute.

1.3

Root cause analysis

Why is dinner a nightly crisis? Because at 5 PM nobody can say what tonight’s dinner is.
Why not? Because no option is prepared — liked, stocked, and scripted — at the moment of decision.
Why is nothing prepared? Because what the family likes, what was bought, and what was intended live in nobody’s head at once.
Why does no such shared memory exist? Because outcomes are never recorded — every dinner vanishes without teaching the system anything.

Four root causes, each mapped to a mechanism in the application:

No preference memoryFamily verdicts on past meals are lost; good meals aren’t repeated, bad ones are.
→ per-person feedback: ratings + tags
Purchases lack intentIngredients are bought unattached to meals — presence in the fridge ≠ a makeable dinner.
→ readiness (have / probably / need) driven by the plan
Decision at the worst momentThe choice lands at peak depletion with zero prepared options.
→ the Cook screen: fit + readiness + steps at 5 PM
Outcomes never recordedNo log of what actually happened — cooked, ordered, split — so nothing improves.
→ meal instances, incl. split-outcome nights
1.4

Hypothesis

If the household runs a low-friction system that (a) remembers which dinners the family actually likes, (b) links grocery purchases to intended meals, and (c) presents ready-to-cook options at the 5 PM moment, then dinner decisions will resolve in under a minute, the home-cooked share of nights will rise, and takeout will shift from an unplanned fallback to a budgeted, deliberate choice.

Corollary: planning does not eliminate uncertainty — mood, weather, energy, and satiety still move the target nightly. The system therefore absorbs uncertainty (pivots, leftovers signals, honest fallbacks) rather than assuming the plan will hold.

1.5

The designed experiment

The application is the experiment apparatus: a mobile-first web app (React + PocketBase, at apps/whos-making-dinner) that instruments the nightly decision.

ElementRole in the experiment
Week zeroBaseline & seed — the four real dinners of Aug 10–13 loaded as data, so the system starts with the household’s actual behavior, not a blank screen. Rating those dinners is the onboarding act.
MeasurementEvery night produces one or more meal instances (what happened, for whom, how) and optional per-person feedback (stars + tags).
InterventionThe week plan and the readiness-driven buy list — buying on purpose — plus the Cook screen presenting prepared options at the decision moment.
RolloutPhase 1: Kyle solo, kinks worked out. Phase 2: Marissa joins; kids rate via parents. Phase 3: the auto-planner drafts the week (variety · nutrition · cost · effort) and Stitch takes conversational entries over Telegram — both already schema-ready.
1.6

Evaluation criteria

MetricSignal ofTarget / direction
Decision time5 PM friction< 1 minute
Nights loggedInstrumentation coverage — nothing else is valid without it≥ 6 of 7 / week
Home-cooked shareAlignment holding through execution↑ from 75% baseline
Fallback ordersfailure outcome — see definition below↓ toward 0
Missing-ingredient events at cook timeBuy-list & readiness accuracy↓ per week
Feedback coveragePreference memory forming≥ 1 rating on most cooked nights
VarietyRepetition fatigue (protein & cuisine rollups)distinct dinners/30d steady or ↑
Waste & spendFull-loop economics (phase 3, needs inventory + cost data)−50% waste / −30% takeout (Holy Grail targets)

Failure outcome, defined. An unplanned order — takeout or delivery chosen at the decision moment because no cookable option was prepared — is the system’s failure signal. It is recorded honestly, never hidden: week zero’s Thursday (Chinese takeout + an Italian restaurant split) is seeded exactly this way and is the worked example throughout this document. A planned restaurant night, or an order taken after a run of consecutive cooking nights, is a budgeted choice — the effort-load context is tracked so the system can tell an earned night off from a collapse of the plan. The goal is not zero orders; it is zero surprised orders.

1.7

Scope boundary

Explicit non-goals, from the product brief — the MVP stays a decision tool, not a kitchen totalization project:

  • Not full pantry management. Readiness is a three-state confidence flag (have / probably / need), sufficient to answer “can we plausibly make this tonight?”
  • Not fairness scorekeeping. Who cooked is recorded as a logistical detail on each night; there is deliberately no per-person scoreboard.
  • Not takeout optimization or household analytics. Orders are recorded and classified; optimizing them is out of scope.
1.8

Risks & constraints

  • Logging fatigue — the whole experiment fails if capture takes over ~30 seconds; every flow is built around one-tap defaults.
  • Cold preferences — early suggestions are only as good as week zero; the system must not act smarter than it is.
  • Infrastructure — the shared PocketBase instance must be reachable over HTTPS for the deployed app; the app degrades to cached data offline.
  • Deploy budget — site deploys are rationed; the app ships as its own Netlify site on Kyle’s action.
2

Data Schema

nine collections · one shared household

The model’s central insight: a meal (a reusable concept — cooked or ordered) is separate from a meal instance (what actually happened on a date). A date can hold several instances — that is how split-outcome nights are first-class. People are members, not accounts, so the kids participate without logins. Every collection carries the same shared-household rule: any authenticated user reads and writes everything.

CollectionPurposeFields that carry the design
dinner_membersThe household — eaters, cooks, ratersname · is_kid · optional link to an auth user
dinner_taxonomyThe ontology: categories, protein types, prep methods, cuisineskind · slug · parent (rollups: poultry→chicken, asian→thai)
dinner_ingredientsIngredients with purchase-intent statereadiness: have / probably / need · is_pantry_staple
dinner_mealsReusable dinner conceptsmeal_kind: cooked / takeout / restaurant · recipe_steps · health_notes · effort · cost_band
dinner_meal_ingredientsWhat a meal needsrole: key / optional / garnish — the buy list runs on key
dinner_meal_instancesWhat actually happened — several rows per date on split nightsmeal_type: cooked / leftovers / takeout / restaurant · participants · cook
dinner_feedbackThe family verdict, per person per nightrating 1–5 · tags: make_again, tweak_it, too_much_effort, kids_complained, great_leftovers
dinner_plansIntent — powers the Cook screen & buy list; the future auto-planner writes herestatus: planned / cooked / skipped · planned_cook
dinner_shopping_extrasOff-plan shopping itemsname · done
example data · week zero

Three meals, as stored

Monday · cooked · stovetop

Creamy Chicken Pasta

key ingredientschicken breast · pasta · bell pepper · broccoli · baby spinach · chicken stock · heavy cream · Parmesan · olive oil · garlic · salt · pepper
recipe steps
  1. Sear seasoned chicken breast and slice
  2. Sauté bell peppers and broccoli
  3. Add chicken stock and cream
  4. Stir in Parmesan until smooth
  5. Toss with cooked pasta, fold chicken back in
  6. Add spinach at the end to wilt
  7. Finish with extra Parmesan and black pepper
health profileHigh protein, substantial; vegetables integrated directly. Cream + Parmesan are the calorie source — lighter than pure cream sauce because stock extends it.
readcomforting · dependable · kid-friendly
Tuesday · cooked · oven roast

Asian-Style Salmon, Fried Rice & Green Beans

key ingredientssalmon fillet (1.61 lb) · Asian-style sauce · leftover cooked rice · cauliflower · bell pepper · green beans · soy sauce · oil + arugula, red cabbage, basil, mint, lime
recipe steps
  1. Coat salmon with sauce and roast
  2. Fried rice from leftover takeout rice, cauliflower, peppers
  3. Season with soy sauce and aromatics
  4. Finish with basil and/or mint
  5. Cook green beans separately
  6. Serve with arugula + cabbage dressed with lime
health profileMost nutritionally balanced of the three: strong protein and omega-3, high vegetable and fiber variety. Sodium is the watchout.
readhealthiest · most composition complexity
Wednesday · cooked · grill

Grilled Skirt Steak, Roasted Baby Yukons, Peppers & Onions

key ingredientsskirt steak (1.75 lb total) · baby Yukon Gold potatoes · bell peppers · onion · olive oil · salt · pepper + steak seasoning
recipe steps
  1. Season skirt steak and let it sit
  2. Roast halved baby Yukons at 425°F
  3. Cook peppers and onions until lightly caramelized
  4. Grill over high heat to medium-rare/medium
  5. Rest; slice thinly against the grain
health profileProtein-rich whole foods; potatoes bring potassium and carbs. Higher red-meat saturated fat than chicken or salmon — portion size drives the profile.
readsimple · satisfying · higher red-meat cost
example data · outcomes

The week-zero instance log

Four nights, five rows — Thursday is two instances on one date. The Mon–Wed rows are the pattern the system exists to extend; the Thursday rows are the failure outcome it exists to reduce: nothing was planned, three straight cooking nights had drained the tank, and the household split into two separate orders.

DateMealmeal_typeParticipantsCookReading
Mon · Aug 10Creamy Chicken PastacookedeveryoneKylealigned
Tue · Aug 11Asian-Style Salmon…cookedeveryoneKylealigned
Wed · Aug 12Grilled Skirt Steak…cookedeveryoneKylealigned · 3rd consecutive
Thu · Aug 13Chinese takeouttakeoutKyle, Rowan, Dylan—fallback · unplanned
Thu · Aug 13Italian restaurantrestaurantMarissa, Hudson—fallback · split night

The nuance the schema preserves: Thursday was also earned — the effort load of three consecutive cooked nights is derivable from the instance log, so the future planner can schedule an easy night or a planned order before the collapse happens. Failure data is the planner’s training signal, which is why it is recorded without judgment.

3

UX Storyboard

seven pathways, one kitchen

Frames below are real screenshots from the running application in demo mode. Six pathways feed one: everything the household logs, plans, buys, and rates converges on the Cook screen, where information becomes dinner.

A

Log a meal

The nightly capture, built for under 30 seconds: pick what happened, confirm who ate and who cooked, done. Ordering out is logged with the same honesty as cooking.

1tonight — tonight’s episode, with best options ranked
→
2pick the meal — recent dinners first, search, or create new
→
3capture the outcome — cooked/leftovers/takeout/restaurant, who ate, who cooked (optional)
→
4as aired — the night is on the record; rating is one tap away
B

Plan the week

Intent, written down. A seven-day strip; each planned dinner immediately powers the Cook screen and the buy list. The future auto-planner writes into exactly this pathway.

1the week ahead — empty days say so, honestly
→
2pick a day, pick a meal — optionally put someone on the hook
→
3on the plan — Saturday has a script now (Marissa’s night)
C

Identify ingredients to purchase

Buying on purpose. The list is computed, not maintained: key ingredients of planned dinners whose readiness is need, ranked by which dinner comes first — plus a pantry check for every “probably have it.”

1a plan exists — chicken pasta, tomorrow
→
2what to buy — missing keys surface by aisle, flagged soon!; the pantry check confirms the maybes before the store
→
3checked off — purchases flip readiness to have; the Cook screen turns green
D

Rate & tag a meal

Preference is a spectrum, captured per person while the plates are still on the table. Kids’ verdicts count — a parent taps them in. This is the memory every future suggestion runs on.

1the retrospective — any night, one tap to the verdict
→
2the family verdict — stars + tags per person: make again, tweak it, too much effort, kids complained, great leftovers
E

Classify the health profile

Every meal carries its own nutritional read — protein, vegetables, watchouts — plus effort, cost band, and kid-friendliness. These are the planner’s future levers for “healthier this week.”

1classify — cuisine, prep method, effort, cost, kid-friendly: taxonomy chips, not typing
→
2the health read — salmon’s profile as stored: balanced, omega-3 strong, sodium the watchout
F

The recipe book

The family menu as a living cookbook: searchable, filterable by cuisine, protein, and effort, every entry carrying its recipe, its ingredients with live readiness dots, and its track record.

1the menu — everything the family knows how to have for dinner
→
2one meal, whole story — steps in order, keys vs nice-to-haves, 🟢🟡🔴 readiness at a glance
G

The Cook screen

Where everything turns into action. The plan supplies the script, feedback supplies the confidence, readiness answers “can we?”, the recipe supplies the next two hours — and the honest fallback is one tap, so even a failure night produces clean data.

1the decision, prepared — best options with family fit and 🔴 missing-ingredient verdicts
→
2how it goes — the recipe unfolds in place; the next two hours are legible
→
3lock it in — or call it and order, on the record either way
→
4the verdict — and tomorrow the system is slightly smarter
